title: NLP Mid-Term
description: 18 questions on tokenization, embeddings, attention, transformers, and language models.

questions.question: Why can't a neural network process raw text directly?
options: Text is too slow to read
Neural networks only operate on numbers; text must first be converted to numerical representations
Text has infinite vocabulary
Neural networks don't support the ASCII standard
questions.explanation: Neural networks compute with real-valued tensors. Raw text (characters or words) must be encoded as vectors — either via lookup embeddings or tokenizer-assigned IDs — before processing.

questions.question: BPE (Byte-Pair Encoding) tokenization starts by treating each character as a token and then:
options: Splits words at every vowel
Randomly merges pairs of tokens
Iteratively merges the most frequent adjacent pair of tokens into a new single token
Uses a dictionary lookup to replace words
questions.explanation: BPE repeatedly finds the most common adjacent pair in the corpus and merges it into one token. After many merges, common words become single tokens while rare ones stay as subword pieces.

questions.question: Subword tokenization (BPE, WordPiece) solves the out-of-vocabulary (OOV) problem because unknown words can always be split into known subword pieces.
questions.explanation: Even a word the model has never seen whole can be broken into characters or known subwords. At worst you fall back to individual characters/bytes, which are always in vocabulary.

questions.question: Word2Vec 'king − man + woman ≈ queen' demonstrates that word embeddings:
options: Can perform arithmetic on words
Encode semantic relationships as geometric directions in the embedding space
Are always exactly 300 dimensions
Were trained on the Wikipedia article about royalty
questions.explanation: The gender direction (man→woman) is a consistent offset in the space. Subtracting 'man' and adding 'woman' moves along that direction, landing near 'queen'. This is semantic algebra.

questions.question: What does cosine similarity measure when comparing two word embeddings?
options: The Euclidean distance between them
The angle between them, capturing directional similarity regardless of magnitude
Whether the words appear in the same sentence
The difference in their token IDs
questions.explanation: Cosine similarity = (a·b) / (|a| |b|). It equals 1 for identical directions, 0 for orthogonal (unrelated), -1 for opposite. It ignores vector magnitude, focusing on direction.

questions.question: In the attention mechanism, what are Query, Key, and Value?
options: Three separate neural networks
Three linear projections of the input: Q asks 'what do I need?', K says 'what do I contain?', V is what gets returned
The three layers of a transformer block
Named after database terminology — they have no specific meaning in attention
questions.explanation: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QKᵀ/√d) V. The Q-K dot product scores relevance; softmax makes them probabilities; then those weights sum the Values. Every token can attend to every other token.

questions.question: Self-attention allows every token in a sequence to attend to (combine information from) every other token in the same sequence.
questions.explanation: Unlike RNNs, which process tokens one at a time, self-attention computes interactions between ALL pairs of tokens simultaneously — enabling long-range dependencies without sequential processing.

questions.question: Why is the attention score divided by √d_k (square root of key dimension) in scaled dot-product attention?
options: To speed up computation
To prevent the dot products from growing so large that softmax gradients become near-zero
To normalize the Query vectors
Because keys have different units from queries
questions.explanation: With large d_k, QKᵀ values can be very large, pushing softmax into a nearly-saturated region with tiny gradients. Dividing by √d_k keeps the values in a reasonable range.

questions.question: Multi-head attention uses h separate Q, K, V projections because:
options: It makes the model h times bigger in parameters
It allows the model to attend to different types of relationships simultaneously in different representation subspaces
It is required to maintain the same sequence length
It prevents gradient vanishing
questions.explanation: Each attention head can specialize — one might focus on syntactic relationships, another on coreference, another on semantics. The heads are concatenated and projected back to the model dimension.

questions.question: BERT is pre-trained with Masked Language Modeling (MLM). What does this mean?
options: Some tokens are replaced with [MASK] and the model predicts the original tokens
All tokens are masked and the model regenerates the entire sentence
The model predicts the next sentence given the current one
The model learns to ignore stop words
questions.explanation: 15% of tokens are randomly masked. BERT is trained to predict those masked tokens using context from both directions (bidirectional). This forces deep contextual understanding.

questions.question: GPT is a decoder-only transformer trained with causal (left-to-right) language modeling — it predicts the next token given all previous tokens.
questions.explanation: GPT uses a causal mask so each position can only attend to earlier positions. Pre-training is to predict token t+1 given tokens 1...t. This makes it natural for text generation.

questions.question: Positional encoding is added to token embeddings in transformers because:
options: Self-attention is permutation invariant — without position info, 'cat sat on mat' and 'mat on sat cat' look identical to the model
It reduces the number of parameters
It replaces the Query-Key computation
It encodes the frequency of each token
questions.explanation: Attention has no built-in notion of order. Without positional encoding, swapping tokens gives identical outputs. Positional encoding injects order information into the representation.

questions.question: Fine-tuning a pre-trained language model means:
options: Training it from scratch on a new task
Continuing training on task-specific labeled data, adapting the pre-trained weights
Freezing all weights and only using the model for feature extraction
Changing the tokenizer to match the new task
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning starts from pre-trained weights (which encode general language knowledge) and continues gradient updates on your task data. Far more efficient than training from scratch.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a [CLS] token in BERT?
options: To mark the end of a sentence
Its final embedding aggregates information from the whole sequence and is used as input to classification heads
It separates two sentences in a sentence-pair task
It stores the attention mask
questions.explanation: BERT prepends [CLS] (class) to every input. After the transformer layers, the [CLS] embedding is a pooled representation of the whole sequence, perfect for classification tasks.

questions.question: Temperature in text generation (T > 1) makes the next-token probability distribution more uniform, increasing diversity but reducing coherence.
questions.explanation: Temperature scales logits before softmax: logits/T. T > 1 flattens the distribution (more random). T < 1 sharpens it (more deterministic). T → 0 is greedy decoding.

questions.question: Transfer learning works for NLP because:
options: Pre-trained models have memorized all possible text
A model trained on large amounts of text learns general linguistic structure and world knowledge that transfers to specific tasks with little data
All NLP tasks share the same labels
Pre-trained embeddings are always frozen during fine-tuning
questions.explanation: Pre-training on web-scale text teaches syntax, semantics, facts, and reasoning patterns. Fine-tuning adapts this knowledge to your specific task and label set — even with just hundreds of examples.

questions.question: Which technique is most commonly used to efficiently fine-tune a large language model without updating all its parameters?
options: Dropout
LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation)
Batch Normalization
Knowledge Distillation
questions.explanation: LoRA freezes the original weights and injects small low-rank adapter matrices. Only those are trained — dramatically reducing trainable parameters (sometimes by 99%) while maintaining quality.

questions.question: Beam search with beam size k in text generation keeps track of:
options: The top k individual tokens at each step
The k highest-probability complete sequences generated so far
k random sequences for diversity
The top k attention heads
questions.explanation: Beam search maintains k candidate sequences (beams) at each step, expanding each by one token and keeping the k overall best hypotheses. Greedy is beam size 1.
